Good evening, everyone. We're delighted to welcome you to CFA UK's eminent speaker series.
And I'm delighted to have with me, Monish Pobrii.
Monish, as many of you know, is a director.
and founder and managing partner of Pabriya investment funds.
Monash is also involved very heavily with the Dukshana Foundation, which does a lot of great charitable
work, particularly when it comes to the field of medical sciences.
And Monash made a transition from being a technologist, or a technology-focused investment
professional, onto investing.
And he follows into, on the path, rather, of Ben Graham, Warren Buffett, and also a mentor of some
in terms of Charlie Munga.
So with that, Monish, we're delighted to welcome you.
For those that don't know us, my name is Brishley Mukabathia, and I'm delighted to be joined by
my colleague Oliver as well.
We're both the co-chairs of CFA UK's Value Investment Special Investing Group.
For those that aren't yet members, or haven't yet renewed the dues for CFA UK,
there's still time to sign up, so please do sign up as well.
With that, Oli, why don't I hand it over to you?
Thanks.
Check it's working.
So Moniz, thank you so much for joining us.
It's very generous of you to come.
And also, your generosity in sharing your ideas on your investing and life, on your books, articles and interviews.
And so I'm sure many here will be familiar with your backstory, but for those less familiar,
or as a reminder, I was going to ask you to walk us through your early years.
your early years and in particular, I was interested in whether having a magician
a magician for a grandfather and an entrepreneur for a father who started many businesses brought you to
where you find yourself today.
Yeah, well, it's wonderful to be here.
Thank you for having me.
I'm glad we could kind of make it work.
I had a short trip to London, and it's nice that we could make this happen.
In many ways, I think I feel like I kind of won the ovarian lottery.
You know, I had wonderful parents.
I would say almost like a dream grandfather.
So my grandfather, he, he, he passed away when I was about 12 years old.
And he was actually a world-famous magician, probably top four or five in the world.
And he actually learned, initially learned his trade here in London, and a British magician named
Owen Clark.
And he was always right till the end trying to continuously improve as a magician and
continuously trying to get better and all.
that. But as a grandfather, you know, in the summers, we used to visit him. He'd take summers off and we'd go to his, my mom's childhood home in the foothills of the Himalayas.
A very nice summers in that place. And he would start the day with doing magic tricks for us. And he was very good at close-up magic.
So there are magicians who, you know, he could actually do many different things, but he was really good at close-up.
So, you know, really close, it's more difficult.
And we would get up in the morning and have all these different tricks and things he'd do.
And then he'd want us to have dessert first.
You know, so then it would immediately go from magic to go to some place which had great desserts.
And of course, he ignored my grandmother and my mother and all of that.
And so it was like his focus was to make sure that all the grandkids have the time of their lives.
So it was really amazing summers with him.
My father was a quintessential entrepreneur.
So he must have started, grown, and bankrupted, at least a dozen companies in a dozen different industries.
And the common theme was that he was really good at identifying offering gaps in the market.
So he was a dozen different industry. And the common theme was that he was really good at identifying offering gaps in the
So he was really good at kind of what was going on and saying, oh, if there was a product or service
like this, it could do well. And it never really stopped him in terms of whether he had competence
in that particular area. So he was really good at quite amazing, quite amazing actually, at figuring
out things in a variety of different industries. One of the ventures that he had
started, which actually was paid for our college education in the U.S. before it went bankrupt.
So it was really good was he started a gold jewelry factory in Dubai.
And he had gone bankrupt, and that bankruptcy in 77 was pretty intense for him.
And he had switched for the first time in several decades to a job.
He'd taken a job in Dubai, some semblance of stability.
And he was on a flight going from Mumbai to Dubai.
And there was this guy in the gold building.
who was sitting next to him, two-hour flight. And by the end of the flight,
they decided to become partners. And they were going to create a new venture. And it was,
again, classically, my dad was just just talked to him about his business. And it turned out that
the UAE had no duties or tariffs on raw gold coming in, but they had a 2%
duty on finished gold coming in in jewelry form. But the 2% was
on the entire value of the jewelry. So if you just looked at the labor content, the duty was much higher,
because most of the content was gold, labor was a small portion. And so the guy who was a jeweler
was telling my dad that, you know, there is no jewelry manufacturing that exists in Dubai or in the
UAE. But if someone were to set up, you know, move the gold.
from India, even though the costs would be higher, there was an arbitrage
because you would, there was a big spread between your elevated costs and what would be the cost
of finished gold coming in.
And that, you know, that's what my father is all about, is the arbitrage spread.
And, and he said, okay, this guy knows the jewelry business.
I understand spreads, and we can do this. And the fact that he had no capital and, you know,
those are always minor details for my dad. And it worked. I mean, basically,
and he was really smart. So I think, I think within, you know, the guy who was his partner was like a third
generation, 70, 80 years in the jewelry business, and kind of grew up with it. And so he had a lot
of knowledge. My dad in about 10 months was equal to him in knowledge. You know, it was
he knew just as much of other businesses as him. And he was actually better than him because
he had done a lot of things in manufacturing, so he was actually able to bring in a bunch
of kind of processes and things which were better than what this guy could do. So that business
actually took off because there was a spread. And then what happened is, which happened with many
of his businesses, is that other people figured out that there's a spread. And then
the second competitor, the third competitor, and then a lot of competitors. And that spread
just vanished basically. And it became really hard. And so then that business in the
event, in the end, basically, there was no, it became a Me Too proposition. But by that time,
we had, I had, my brother and had completed about two-thirds. We had two-thirds of our way through
a degree when he went bankrupt. And then my, one of my uncles helped us with helping us finish
college and such. So, but anyway, that business, which was basically happening from the time I was, like,
about 14 or 15 onwards. He used to take me on sales calls with him when I was
about 16. I really don't know why he did that because I was a kind of squawny, underweight kid,
not any charisma for sales or anything, and it would be kind of strange, you know, you're going to walk
into it. He'd be cold calling these jewelers, and, you know, you're walking in with a teenager,
and he didn't care about all that. But to me, it taught me a lot because I just saw
how he'd walk into store where he doesn't know anyone, doesn't, they don't know him,
and he'd close deals, you know, and jewelry is a big trust business. You know, people have to really
trust you. And he was able to build that pretty quickly. So anyway, I felt like by the time I
I was 18 because, you know, so many of these businesses been bankrupt and I think when
my brother and I were 12 or 13. We used to sit down with him. We were like
as board of directors at night, and we had to figure out how to make the business last for one more
day. You know, everything, all the walls were caving in and the business was dying and we were just
trying to make it last for one more day. And then we'd make it last for one more day
and then next night sit down and how do we make it last for one more day. And
so I finished several MBAs by the time I was 18.
And in looking back, you know, there was no kind of plan for any of this, but looking
back, it was without that experience, I wouldn't have been able to be an investor.
It helped me, I think what happened is, and I didn't even know I had this skill, but I can crack
business models really fast in a lot of industries that I may not have seen before
and such, because they got so much exposure in those years. So I'm very grateful.
that's fascinating. Thanks. So fast-forward a bit. You became an employee
at Telabs and then moved into international sales and marketing and eventually founded your own business.
Do you want to talk about a bit of that journey? Maybe to the point where you sold a minority
state to... All the turmoil I had seen when I was in childhood, because my parents were really bad.
financial planners, you know. So basically, when the business
went bankrupt, there was no money for rent or groceries or anything. So, you know, they're
trying to borrow from family and friends. And it was pretty traumatic. And so
my take was that once I got my degree, engineering and such, I knew that I would have
good job prospects, a good career, decent income, you know, put away 15% in a
retirement plan and let a compound and so on. So I really would have a good job prospects, a good career, decent income,
really had no interest in ever being an entrepreneur. I just didn't like all the huge
gyrations that I had seen. So that's what I had resigned myself to. That's what I was doing. And my dad
was visiting me, I think I was 24, and he told me one day that it's time to quit and
start your own thing. And I said, you know, don't you remember my childhood, you know, it's not
not the path I want to go down. He said, all I remember was a lot of excitement, you know.
And he said to me, he said, look, you know, there are only two kinds of people who matter in a company, large business.
He says, the people who create have got some kind of role in the creation of the product or service, and the people who sell.
So he said a business is the people who create, the people who sell, and then a lot of fill in the blanks in the middle, okay?
So he said, number one, you never want to be in the middle.
So he said, you either want to be on the creative side or you want to be on the selling side, if you want to work for someone.
And then he said, I was at that time on the selling side.
So he said, look, and before that, I was on the creative side and the R&D side.
So when I was in R&D, he actually told me, look, you could drop dead tomorrow, and they wouldn't even know that that's happened.
They wouldn't even miss you.
So even whatever you bring to the party on the creative side is basically me too.
And he helped me move to the other side because he said, even if you're a mediocre sales guy doing something,
you have value to the business.
So I actually moved to international marketing and sales.
And then he told me, look, it's good that you made the move from creative to selling, but all the spoils go to someone else.
You know, you don't really see much of the spoils.
And really, you need to cash.
more of the spoils for yourself.
And I was getting bored with the bureaucracy, it was getting bigger, and so on.
And so I decided, yeah, maybe he's right.
I'll take the plunge.
I tried to make it as low risk as possible.
And then I found an offering gap because I knew how to find offering gaps.
I can find offering gaps really easily.
And even Pabrii funds was an offering gap.
So basically went down the path and then basically
accidentally heard about Warren Buffett and Charlie Bunger
in exactly about 30 years ago.
And that was a big eye-opener for me because I said, wow, this is really cool because you're basically using the same brain cells
to do investment research as you would to figure out strategy in a business that you're running.
I thought it would be more interesting and more leverage to apply those brain cells in investing
because you wouldn't have to do any execution.
So I always enjoyed the strategy part of the businesses much more than the execution part.
Execution is a lot of heavy lifting.
is a lot of heavy lifting. It's fun the first few times, but it's better to be on the...
I always like to try to figure the business out.
And so the big aha moment for me with Warren Buffett was that all he does is figure businesses out.
He doesn't really run them.
And so that's how I made, I tried to see if I could make that transition.
And I did it being an investor for myself.
I sold a small portion of the company.
I had a million dollars for the first time I had cash in the bank.
And about five years later, the million was about 13 million.
And so the public investing went way better than I thought, kind of 94 to 2000.
And then that led to the formation of Pabrii Fund and then I kind of went from there.
So that's an interesting one moment.
Just very quickly.
You mentioned about that low risk and that offer and gap piece.
And you talked about the menteeship that you had, say, from Charlie Munger
and Warren Buffett, how do you sort of look at that offer gap as well as, say, those
low-risk scenarios and sectors that might not necessarily be ones that you would have traditionally
focused in? What would be your suggestions to say someone that's maybe young and starting out
in the industry for the first time, or maybe even to experience investors?
Well, I mean, I think our job is to look for anomalies, and our job is investors
to look for things that make no sense. It's when things make no sense that
that's when there's some opportunity.
So on a steady state basis, I think that markets are mostly efficient.
You know, if you have a business like Coca-Cola, and, you know, they sell syrup to bottleers,
and they've got a dominant brand all over the world, it's unlikely that a business like that would
trade for one-time's earnings most of the time.
And it's unlikely it would even trade for 10 times earnings.
And, you know, sometimes things get euphoric, and it may trade for 40-50 times earnings like it did in like it did in, like, 99, 2000.
And sometimes things get kind of pessimistic, like I think, in the early 70s and until the early 80s and until the early 80s where it's trading at seven times earnings or such.
So it vacillates.
And so when a business like that gets to the low-end extreme of being very undervalued, then that's
interesting. And because there are 50,000 stocks, you know, I don't like to quote
Jim Kramer too much, but, you know, he says there's always a bull market somewhere. And, you know,
I mean, I think he's right in a way, in a way that there's always, it's not possible that in a global market
of 50,000 or so trade and equities that everything is perfectly priced. You, there's a nature of
markets that they're going to undershoot and overshoot. And in fact, if you just, you know,
throw darts on all the businesses in the London Stock Exchange or the New York
Stock Exchange, any random company that you, the dart hits, you look at the 52-week range on that stock,
it's going to be like 60 to 100, or like 75 to 125 or 75 to 150.
And it's not possible for most businesses that there's that much value change happening
in a year. You know, the Coke business doesn't change that much in a year. But the stock price,
because it's auction-driven markets, the nature of auction-driven markets is that the way the mechanism
by which prices get set can have a deviation from underlying fundamentals. And so that's what allows us
to actually make a living. That's what we do. So there's always things that are going on
in markets. And I've always felt that, you know, whatever criteria, you know, whatever
you said that I only want to buy things that are at a trailing P.E.
You would find those. If you said that I only want to buy things at a trailing P.E.E. of 0.1, you would find those too.
And if you said, I only want to buy things at one-third of book value, you would find those as well.
So you can set any criteria you want and Mr. Market will give you
give you companies that fit that criteria. And then you can drill down and
see whether that kind of works for you or doesn't work for you. Take it from there.
Would you be able to describe a bit the, when you generated the growth from 1 to 13 million
and maybe in your first few years running the PAPRIF? Was it, would you say it's more
deep value or if you don't want to label it if you don't want to label it,
but deep value special situations or were there quality companies as well in that?
Yeah. So when I first started out as an investor, I spent a lot of time reading up on Warren
Buffett and Charlie Munger and the Berkshire Annual Reports and all of that. And because I was running
this IT business, I was, my circle of competence was very heavily technology. And technology basically
has the nuance of having high returns on equity for the most part. And technology basically has the nuance of having high returns
on equity for the most part. And it's a good place to be. So as long as you're
not paying too much, you know, it's always great to be in businesses that have growth and that have high
returns on equity. And so from like 94 to about 99 or 2000, I was very much a growth investor
because I understood kind of that's what kind of was front and center of my, so
Almost the entire portfolio was tech at that time, probably 80, 90% was tech.
But I got concerned. I had privately started a dot com and it failed. And that was painful. I mean, I lost about
$3 million. I had some outside investors that lost about $2 million. But what that gave me was it gave me was it gave me
about a three-month look ahead versus what the market could see. So I could see that we were in a very big bubble in a very big bubble in early 2000,
99. And I didn't know when it would blow and how it would blow, but I was pretty
sure at some point this party would come to come to an end. So what I did is Pabraifan started in in July
99 and I made a complete switch at that point. So I went from, you know, these great
businesses in tech and so on because they've become just so frothy to deep value. And in fact,
The day the NASDAQA peaked, I think March 9, 2000, was the day Berkshire hit a multi-year low.
So people were literally selling Berkshire to buy Pets.com and Chemdex.com and whatever else was happening then.
And so very simple, stable businesses in the markets became hated and unloved. And they became
really cheap. And so I was buying funeral homes and, you know, companies having oil tankers,
and that sort of thing. And we did really well. I mean, I think the
NASDAQ crashed and burned. And Pabri Funds, I think from 99 to like 2007, we did, before fees,
we did 37% a year. No down years for about eight years. And it was done with a bunch of very
basic non-growth type businesses. And of course, what I needed to do, which I got so
comfortable with the deep value and all of that is that probably by around 2,000,
11 or 12, I should have switched back because by that time all the froth and stuff
had gone away, but I'd become so comfortable in this. So I was about six years late in actually
realizing I need to kind of go back to the better businesses and so on. But, you know,
it's a forgiving business, so life is okay. Just on that theme that you'd mentioned about,
say, looking at deep value versus growth, do you find any resonances right now?
would say the AI theme or deep growth and how does one, if you do, how does one
cut away the noise from looking with say versus looking at true value-oriented sectors or companies?
Yeah, so actually value and growth are joined at the hip. It's like a coin with two sides.
Really cannot think of them differently. So all businesses are worth the sum of future
cash they produce discounted to present value at some reasonable interest rate.
And so it doesn't matter whether you're looking at NVIDIA or some funeral home or, you know, any business.
Any business has a very clear-cut, single definition of what it's worth.
The controversies come in on what are those cash flows and how certain are you.
And I think that's where the difficulties come in because businesses by their very nature are very unpredictable.
I mean, there's a wide range of things that can happen to a business over time and especially
the further out you go in the years. I mean, the insiders of
NVIDIA couldn't tell us what it looks like five or ten years from now in terms of revenues
and cash flows. They might have some difficulties with that. So people on the outside looking in
would have even greater difficulties. But basically, I don't particularly, you know, go one
way or another. I'm open to, it's always better to be invested in a business which has
growth prospects and has high returns and equity. It could be better to do that
and even pay a higher multiple than a very low P.E.E. on something that's flat or declining. So the bias
should always be towards a great growing business. But one should kind of be agnostic. It should
just look at the landscape and kind of see what's going on. And so your philosophy, so your philosophy it sounds
like it's sort of, well, Whitney Tilton calls himself on make money
investor, rather than value or growth. And over the years with Pagbrii funds, have you found certain
sectors that you've done better in or worse in? Or has it really been start agnostic, sector agnostic,
just look for opportunities? It's a really opportunistic business. So one of the things
Charlie would repeatedly tell me. I think people asked Warren and Charlie this question that,
you guys were starting today, you know, how would you do? And his answer
what we would do terribly, you know, because he said that, you know, in the 60s or 70s, they were shooting fish in a
barrel after letting the water out, you know. And so they had so many opportunities. I mean, U.S.
markets, you know, 74, 75, that was an orgasmic period to be a value investor, you know.
It was just unbelievable.
You could pretty much bought anything and you would have done well.
And equities were, you know, just primed to do well for the next couple of decades.
So today, I think Charlie and Warren always complained that the brainpower that is focused on, you know,
public equities and all of that is very significant.
I mean, you know, we have more mutual funds than stocks in the U.S., probably similar in the U.
and we have more hedge funds than stocks.
And so the thing is that, and we have more analysts than stocks, by some factor, you know, maybe three to one or four to one or something.
So a lot of stuff is picked over.
I found the last few years it's quite difficult to find stuff.
And, you know, when I look at my portfolio currently, it's the most weird portfolio you can think of.
You know, I manage about a billion dollars.
is about 600 million in Turkey in three names, another 300 million in coal,
in three or four names, and a few other things, which don't matter that much.
You know, and I would have never guessed that would be kind of, you know, that way.
But to tell you, just to tell you how weird and opportunistic this business is,
I had at 13 months ago, 13 months ago, 13 months back,
my investments in coal was zero.
I had no investments in the coal business.
Just around 13 months ago, maybe, yeah, just about 13 months ago, March, May 18th or so.
I saw a tweet on Twitter, where someone had put my handle on the tweet and said,

I have very fond memories of.
So when I saw that tweet, I actually, in my mind, I thought that even though God loves me,
he doesn't love me so much to give me a second Ipsco.
It's like one and done.
And that what had happened in 2003 and 2004 was never going to happen in my lifetime again.

They made steel for pipelines and oil fields and so on.
And it was a company with no debt.
They had $15 dollars a share in cash.
And they had given guidance that for the next two years, our net income and free cash flows
are going to be $15 dollars a year for each year.
for the stock was at $40.
So if you just look to the cash on the balance sheet and the next two years of cash coming in, you
you would be at $45 and plant and equipment and inventory would all be free.
There was no debt.
And they were giving this, this was not really guidance because when these people built pipelines,

these were firm purchase orders. And so the company had extreme clarity on exactly what they

It was possible that after two years, cash flows could be zero, could be negative.
But I said, you know, why, why, for
on the negative, you know, let's keep them, like my dad, let's always
think the glass is overflowing, you know. And so I said the extent of the analysis I did was,
I just want to own this for two years, and I just want to see what Mr. Market prices this

doubled. And we still have this issue where it's a very cyclical business and who
knows what happens. And I was thinking, you know, we should, we've got long-term gains.

and the stocks at 155, some Swedish company offered to buy it for $160 a share. And I don't
know why the Swedes didn't come a year earlier and buy it for $60 a share. But, you know,
things don't make sense on this planet, you know? Like Mark Twain says, you know, fiction
fiction makes sense, but reality never makes sense. So one femtosecond after reading that, I unloaded
the shares. And so when I'm reading this tweet, someone says, Ipso is back. And, you know, that's
a wonderful life. So I said, let's look into console energy, which I've never heard of in my life.
And I looked into it.
And I realized that there were some differences, but there was a big positive in console,
which was not there in Ipsco. Console, console was furiously buying back shares. If Ipsco was doing
buybacks, it would have been on steroids. You know, I mean, that would have been something,
there would have been a sight to behold. But, you know, there were very few management teams
